utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, before I continue, I would like to ask you whether you have considered the possibility of giving me some additional time, because Lord Owen was the main international negotiator for three years, and it is impossible to cover in three hours even very superficially the main issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've considered the position as we did -- as we said yesterday. You have one session, an hour and a half. I suggest that one way you can save time is by keeping your questions short, concentrating and focusing on them rather than lengthy questions. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lord Owen, yesterday we ended the session with your position about the crimes committed by the Serbs in response to my statement that crimes were committed by all sides. I hope that you will recollect that we had discussed those camps in Bosnia and Herzegovina and that you will remember, I hope, that both you and Stoltenberg and myself and other participants, Bulatovic in the first place, received assurances from the leadership of Republika Srpska, that apart from prisoners of war and regular prisons, there was nothing else there, and that even Radovan Karadzic called on Paddy Ashdown publicly to come and see for himself, which he did, after which he made a statement saying that what had appeared in the press was not correct. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first part of our conversations with Dr. Karadzic I certainly do remember, and they were along those lines, and we were given in our negotiating sessions many assurances either about the camps or about the hostages, those people who were taken prisoner. So it is perfectly true to say that those issues were very frequently raised, first by myself and Mr. Vance and then by Mr. Stoltenberg and myself. And it's also true to say that you urged them to make sure that their practices were acceptable to us and to the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that the International Red Cross should be present everywhere and that all prisoners should be exchanged on the principle all for all. Wasn't that how it was, Lord Owen?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly you were always keen to involve the international -- ICRC, and you did in fact see the head of the ICRC from time to time. And I think that they did. We got very much better access to the prison camps. The situation was very much worse when I first arrived in early September 1992. I think it did improve, though. I must say from what I've heard since, the improvements were not what we were assured -- they were not as good as the assurances, put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But my impression was, and I hope you shared it, because a long time after the war information started arriving that there were various violations of international law and various crimes committed in some prisons, that at the time in those days the leadership of Republika Srpska, I mean Karadzic, Krajisnik, Koljevic and others, even they were not aware of those violations, because they assured us to that effect. And my impression was that they were sincere in doing that. Was that your impression too?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think a change took place in Dr. Karadzic. In the early days, in 1992 and in 1993, he seemed to have some understanding about the pressure of the international opinion on human rights questions. And for example, if somebody was taken prisoner, a foreign -- or somebody -- and we made representations about it, he was at pains to make clear that this was not hostage-taking, that this was a purely criminal matter and would be dealt with in the criminal -- by the criminal procedures and that he as president had no involvement with it. And in those early days, I think it seemed to have a ring of conviction to it, but more he was able to flout international opinion on the battlefield and the more he was able to see off plan after plan, the more he became, in my view, less trustworthy and more flagrant about these were not just prisoners, these were hostages. And we had a lot of problems with him in 1994 and early 1995 with hostage-taking, and it was much more obvious that these were -- to my mind that these were political hostages, they were not criminal positions. But you were aware of that, and maybe -- but we could do no more. We would receive these assurances from Dr. Karadzic. All I can say is I couldn't agree with your view that his pledges were sincere. I think increasingly that they came less -- they had carried less conviction and less sincerity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot go into any judgement as to what extent it was sincere because my impression was that they were sincere. But if you remember, some delegations when they came to Serbia even, they asked questions about camps in Serbia. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can't say I've got a complete recall of it, but I think I remember discussions about camps in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that when such an absurd assertion was made I denied it, not only by offering my guarantees that there were no such camps, but I would offer each delegation that may raise such an issue to use a police helicopter to point on the map a spot where they have suspicions that there were such camps to see for themselves that there were no such things. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, but I have no reason to doubt. At that time, I think you were pretty confident about what was exactly happening in the country which you were responsible for, Serbia and then the FRY. But the area of Serbia Montenegro, you knew what was going on. I'm not sure -- I've never doubted that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But surely you know full well that there were no camps in the territory of Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem of professing to knowledge that I don't have, I don't -- it's not an issue which came on my radar screen massively, to be honest. My main focus was on camps in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time. I think that I was focusing on abuses of human rights in Croatia and Kosovo and in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was often taking up with you abuses of human rights in Kosovo, and as you know, I did not agree with a lot of what was happening in -- under Serbian control of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Kosovo is a separate issue. It's a principled matter. I considered Kosovo to be our own internal affair, and it had nothing to do with the war in Bosnia and Croatia and, generally speaking, with the events connected with the break-up of Yugoslavia. You knew that.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that was your view. Of course, I disagreed with it. We had to reach a sort of modus vivendi about that. I think you did accept that the terms of reference of the London conference, which you accepted, did mean that ICFY had -- the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia -- did have a locus on Kosovo, and so you never ruled out talking about it, but you made it abundantly clear that you disliked talking about it and didn't really consider that we had a right to be involved. But we're not really here to talk about Kosovo, but inasmuch as we had a dialogue about Kosovo it was the least satisfactory dialogue that we had. I think you'd agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We didn't discuss that at all because I considered that to be our internal affair.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not my recollection. We did discuss Kosovo. You did often say that it was your internal affair, but neither myself, Mr. Stoltenberg, or Mr. Vance accepted that. But this was an area of very serious disagreement between us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That we had disagreements over that, that is quite true, and I'm not denying it. Lord Owen, I should like to make the best of the time available to me, which is very limited, as you can see, to raise a number of issues, and I would like to ask you kindly to assist me by giving me short answers, if possible. First of all, regarding the nature of the war. In several places in your book, you refer to the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as well as the other wars in the territory of the former Yugoslavia from 1991 to 1995 as civil and a war of secession. For example, on page 5, paragraph 1 -- I have this compact disk that was given to me by the opposite side, and that is why the pagination does not agree with pagination of your book, and I am sorry. You say that, "All wars bring evil to the surface and especially the cruelty of civil wars as recorded through history. It is a fact that the wars in the former Yugoslavia had elements of secessionist and civil wars and this only contributed to the difficulty of making objective judgements." Did you experience those wars as secessionist and civil wars?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were elements of aggression in it. Particularly, it was not possible to classify it as a civil war once the international community had accepted the independence of many of what were hitherto republics in the regions in the former Yugoslavia. But I do not deny in my book talking about aspects of the war that were civil wars, and I think that this is one of the things that the world community never quite understood, or significant sections of it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I also think that they didn't understand, and that is why your explanation is so useful, because you are the most competent person to provide it. In view of the fact that we established yesterday that the Yugoslav People's Army was positioned throughout its territory and that after the recognition of the republics, it pulled out of Croatia when the Vance Plan was adopted and the UN arrived from Bosnia and Herzegovina in the period we indicated yesterday and that the army of Republika Srpska was formed. So in those days, there were no foreign soldiers there, at least not from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is from Serbia and Montenegro. I assume you remember that well. And before that, there was Yugoslavia, the country was Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I -- it's a complex history. I don't claim to have ever fully mastered it, but it was an extremely important part of my task to try to understand how Yugoslavia had come into existence, how the boundaries of -- internal boundaries of the nations and regions of Yugoslavia had been established, how the maps had been drawn up, and I don't dissent from what you're saying, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not reading from your book, but I have a chronology of documents here. But you will probably remember on the 23rd of July, 1993, according to this chronology, co-chairman of the ICFY, Lord David Owen, rejected the possibility of military intervention in Bosnia and Herzegovina and explained it by saying that it was very difficult to intervene in a situation which is not one of aggression. And then your words are cited: "Though this war started partially in that way, but it was always a conflict between the Serbs from Bosnia, the Croats from Bosnia, and the Muslims from Bosnia." That is what you said in July 1993. I assume you remember that.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I unfortunately don't recall every word that I've ever uttered, but I think principally the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina was between those who lived there, but it would be foolish to believe that that was the only aspect of this war. There was, throughout the period that I was involved, JNA forces, people who were not born in Bosnia-Herzegovina operating inside Bosnia-Herzegovina and being helped and aided by the Yugoslav army. And similarly, there were substantial forces from Croatia operating alongside Croatian Serbs and supplying them with arms and ammunition. And therefore, the two states that were bordering Bosnia-Herzegovina that had previously been in the former Yugoslavia as one, namely Serbia, Montenegro, and Croatia, were involved in this war and that was one of the aspects of why it was a civil war. It was a civil war across the former Yugoslavia as well as a civil war within Bosnia-Herzegovina. And then the war had to change in terms of the international community, which I think you and many other Serbs found very difficult, and a good many Croats too. But once recognition had taken place, then there had to be a change. These countries had to be treated as independent countries. We can argue about recognition, but the right of the international community to declare a state which is dissolving itself, to declare certain elements from it now to be independent is there in the UN Charter, and that took place. And that did change the situation. Therefore, from that moment on, any activity from a country outside Bosnia-Herzegovina had, in the eyes of international law, was an aggression, was no longer a civil war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That would be true if we had had troops in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina after the recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but you know that we didn't have any troops in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I even told you and Mr. Stoltenberg of only one exception, and that is that I had sent a police platoon to the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is at the Strpce railway station where a crime was committed, where people were taken off the train on the Belgrade-Bar railway line, to guard that station. And this was in the territory of Republika Srpska, but we feared that some paramilitary units may commit another crime, and they guarded that station, because it is only nine kilometres of the Belgrade-Bar railway line that runs through Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I informed you and Mr. Stoltenberg about this. This was an exception. This was a police platoon that stood guard at the police station to prevent anyone from stopping the train there. This was a station that trains did not stop at normally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, I warned you about time which you're taking up. What is the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember the incident, and I don't think it has much bearing on all of this, but it is a fact that the railway line chipped into Bosnia-Herzegovina for a very small portion. I think it was something like nine kilometres, maybe a bit longer than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That was the exception, that is the presence of this police platoon, and I informed you of that because there were no other Yugoslav forces in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I assume you remember that.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember your interpretation, and we went over yesterday why I disagree with it. I think there was a rather clever way of taking Yugoslav forces into, buttressing the Bosnian Serbian army without it being quite as apparent as, for example, in Croatia. In Croatia, it was completely apparent at some stages in the war. Their forces were without any question whole -- whole detachments deployed into Bosnia-Herzegovina. You went through rather more of a subterfuge, but I do not accept your interpretation that there were no people fighting in the Serb side in Bosnia who could not normally be thought to have been and should have been part of the JNA in -- answerable to you in Serbia and Montenegro. But I may be wrong. But that was the view I held, and I held it consistently, and I think there is some evidence at the time which we based our views on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You never had any objection to the effect that any unit of the JNA was operating in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina; isn't that right? You talked to me on innumerable occasions.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again, I want to reiterate, I don't think you did send formed units from Yugoslavia into Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was much more that people were serving who were not always residents in Bosnia-Herzegovina, they were not people who had spent their whole life there, and that there was a mixing of the two. But I -- I notice your denial, and no doubt there will be evidence given in this court about this matter. I can only tell you what I thought at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you consider those people to be volunteers, those people who went there? You know very well there were many people from Sandzak fighting in the army of Alija Izetbegovic in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were from Serbia, but I assume they were not sent there by Serbia, so the question of volunteers is quite a separate issue.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is a separate issue, and that certainly did happen, and it is also the case, I remember in Sarajevo, being proudly introduced by the Bosnian government force commander to a Serb general who had voluntarily served in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So this is one of the reasons why this war was very complex, and they were not simple questions and simple issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Quite so. On page 552, you say that one of the greatest historians, Thucydides, said that, "People went to war because of fear, honour, and interest. Rarely are there only culprits and victims. This even applies to interstate wars when wars are absolutely or partially civil wars as was the case with the four wars waged in the former Yugoslavia so far, we are wrong to view these matters in simplified terms or to present them as a battle between good and bad guys. So it's far more complex than that." Which four wars are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was always some definition problems. There was an initial war, but sometimes called the war between Serbia and Slovenia. That lasted, if one thought that was a separate war, for a matter of weeks, and that ended. Then there was a war between Serbia and Croatia, and that was highlighted, of course, by the sieges that went on and particularly the long siege of Vukovar. That was the time when the sanctions and the ban on the transfer of weapons into the former Yugoslavia actually hurt the Croatians, and so we need to remember that. Then later, of course, probably preferentially hurt the Bosnian Muslims. And then there was the war between Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, and there was then the war which we can argue about the definition of what -- whether it was purely the Republika Srpska. And then there was an internal war between the Croatian -- the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims which raged in the -- on a couple of occasions very badly in April of -- in the spring of -- April 1993 and then broke out again in 1994, early 1994. And then you go on to the war of -- over Kosovo. So there is a lot of definition of how many separate wars there were, but they all had a common theme in the dissolution of the former Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was a united war against Yugoslavia, and that's how Yugoslavia was broken up. But I don't understand where you get Serbia's war with Slovenia from. It had nothing to do with the intervention of the army in Slovenia. It was up to the federal government, and I assume you know that at least.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- it's -- it's a part of history which I was not a direct participant in, and I don't see much advantage in us locking on that particular question. You may have a different interpretation, certainly very much more knowledge than I have exactly what went on. My interpretation has been that it was a war which was paving the way for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. dissolution, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's quite true. It was a very detrimental war, but Serbia had nothing to do with that particular war, and we didn't even know that the intervention would take place. And as far as Croatia is concerned, well, I have here a letter that I addressed to Cyrus Vance, and that was after several rounds of negotiations that we had. And the letter is dated the 24th of November, 1991, that is to say, even before recognition took place. It was still Yugoslavia that we were dealing with. And he wrote to me on the 24th of November and I answered his letter on the 27th of November. I've mixed up the dates. I apologise for that. But anyway, that was how it was. And I say I wish to express my agreement with respect to the importance of the topics you express interest for in your letter, that is to say the definition of territories under the protection of the United Nations forces, because without doubt, it was my personal support and Serbia's support and the support of the presidents of Yugoslavia that the Blue Helmets came to Croatia in the first place. So I say that there in view of the fact that the definition of territories on which once again an attempt was made and, unfortunately, to a certain extent implemented, genocide over the Serb people, and this led to large scale conflicts. The definition of territories is a de facto question, and I think that the state on the ground is the only objective response, because he was interested in knowing where the UN people should be deployed. And I say that the overall territory, in my view, where the conflicts and clashes took place should enjoy effective protection by the United Nations. And I go on to explain that as the freedom and security and safety of the people living there are vital to the -- their existential interests, I therefore consider that every definition of territory must be checked out and confirmed on the ground, that is to say where the conflicts actually took place. And I go on to emphasise the importance of the decisions made by the Yugoslav state Presidency in this regard, in the interests of understanding --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. There is a limit to what the witness can deal with, what any witness can deal with. What is it that you want to put, Mr. Milosevic? What are you putting? You're asking the witness questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am putting before the witness questions and asking him whether it is true and correct that in the areas populated by the Serbs there were great -- there was great retaliation vis-a-vis the Serbs, that they rebelled and that Yugoslavia, from the very beginning, endeavoured to prevent the conflict there. When I say "Yugoslavia," I mean the Yugoslav People's Army as well and the country's federal institutions which still existed at the time, and that we always strove and advocated for impartiality, and therefore wanted the UN mission to arrive on the spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Again, you're putting a whole lot of things here together. The first point you put is that there was great retaliation vis-a-vis the Serbs in the areas which were populated by them. That's one point. And then you put that Yugoslavia, from the beginning, endeavoured to prevent the conflict there, i.e., the Yugoslav People's Army. I don't know if Lord Owen feels he can comment on that particular proposition.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not involved at this time, but of course Cyrus Vance was a great friend of mine and we discussed the issue. On the point you raised about whether you were helpful to Mr. Vance in those negotiations, of course he's not alive now to answer this question, but I gather that his assistant, Mr. Ambassador Okun, did give evidence here, and I'm sure he would have been able to deal with this. It was certainly my view that Mr. Vance felt that you had been extremely helpful in those negotiations, so I don't wish to dissent from that. On the second round of questions, this whole business of the fact that there were substantial Serb communities, not just in Bosnia-Herzegovina but also in Croatia, that is an undoubted fact. And of course the UN protected areas that came in as part of the plan in Croatia were an attempt to deal with this issue. But the absence of serious negotiations, the absence of getting agreement in Bosnia-Herzegovina which would have helped settle the problems in Croatia resulted in the mass exodus of Serbs from the Krajina. And I think all this demonstrates that we can go over the history -- and this region has got so much history that it bedevils dealing with the future. And all I can say to you is you have a justified grievance, in my view, that the Western world took a view that the only way to create independent countries out of the former Yugoslavia was to accept the regional map of Yugoslavia as drawn up during the war in 1944 by, amongst others, Mr. Djilas. Now, I think that is a perfectly justified grievance, and I've always made it quite clear that I think we should have been readier to have made some changes to those maps in order to reflect some of the long-standing settlement of individuals, Croats and particularly Serbs. But that was not the decision that was made in 1991 by the European Union, and my book makes reference to that very fateful decision. But that was taken in good faith in believing it would not be possible to reach agreement on any other boundaries, and probably that judgement was correct, but I think it did give a grievance to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I have to hurry up. Now, on page 274, you refer to Ratko Mladic and say that, "When in June 1991 the Serbo-Croatian war began, he was the Chief of Staff of the 9th Army Corps, located in Knin. And like the other corps, this one was in the process of dissolving because the officers and staff began to come out and say they were Croats and step down from the JNA to join their national armies. They left the military service, and in some cases, they even left the country. Mostly the Serbs who stayed on in the JNA did not have any freedom and many were surrounded by the Croatian army in their barracks, which was one of the reasons for which the JNA reacted with such force in places like Vukovar. And from that stage, we see the development of a classical civil war with rifts in the army and rifts in friendships between officers from the same regiment and them leaving and going to fight each other." End of quotation. It was the war that flared up in 1991, and you call it a classical civil war, Lord Owen, don't you? Now, can we conclude from that the divisions and rifts in an army of a country that you have described in the way you have where everybody was the member of one and the same army and now suddenly they were beginning to fight each other, that those are properties and traits of a civil war, no other type of war. It was a civil war, in fact. What other type of war could have been waged between the members of the same army who had split and started fighting each other?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I agree with the wording that I used in the book, not perhaps surprisingly, and what you've quoted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment. There's a matter I want to say. It would be helpful if the Prosecution, since you produce these documents, can refer us in due course to these passages which have been referred to from the CD-ROM so we can tie them up with our own copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We will make arrangements. I don't think --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll make arrangements, not necessarily today but as soon as I can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reference, Your Honour, is page 165 and 166. .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Lord Owen. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, if it was indeed a civil war and a war of secession, I assume it's clear that the blame for the war lies with the side conducting the secession and conducting it by using force, this illegal secession. So was that called in question, Lord Owen?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's a gross simplification of the complex background in which you were seeing substantial divisions of opinion in the governing structure of the former Republic of Yugoslavia. You had, as you know very well since you participated in it, a rotating Presidency, and I think many of the Tito structures broke down not just with the outcome of -- with the start of the war but in the months and even years before war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I should like now, because of the shortness of time -- something seems to be wrong with this microphone. Anyway, I should just like -- just to round off this issue and reference to Croatia: On the 16th of July, 1993, I have a notation here saying that the media informed and the government of Croatia and Serbian Krajina signed an agreement in Erdut binding Croatia to withdraw its troops by the 31st of July from the occupied territories of Srpska Krajina, Ravni Kotor, and Maslenica, the Miljevac Plateau, the Peruca hydroelectric power station, and the Zemunik airport in exchange for the opening up of the bridge across the Maslenica canal and the Zemunik airport. And then it goes on to say that the president of the Republic of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic, as well as Franjo Tudjman, the Croatian president, after the meeting held and organised by the co-chairmen of the conference on Yugoslavia, ICFY, Thorvald Stoltenberg and David Owen, made a statement and among other things -- I'm going to skip over this next portion here and go on to point 3 -- expressing their satisfaction with the solutions reached with respect to the Maslenica Bridge, Zemunik and Peruca, the presidents welcome the agreement reached on the cease to hostilities and consider that each individual or group violating that agreement must be held accountable. They indicate the importance of the agreement reached -- the presidents indicate the importance of the agreement reached as an example of how issues should be solved peacefully and consider it to be an important step towards normalising Serbo-Croatian relations as a whole. Now, then, is it true that after the UNPA zones came into being that there were no cases of any kind of instances where Serb forces from the Republika Srpska Krajina attacked any territory outside the protected areas? And as you can see, there were very considerable violations of the PA zones by the Croatian forces. But we did our best to do away with that practice. Isn't that right, Lord Owen?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the court will need to take evidence from the various UN commanders of UNPROFOR in Zagreb. That's -- you're asking a degree of detail which I can't verify either one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us now move on to another topic. Let me tell you of my intentions, to make it easier for you, and the topic is Greater Serbia. There are several places in the book and in a telegram you talk about the idea of a Greater Serbia and mention my name in that regard, and that was expected in view of the frightening propaganda and demonisation that was going on in the Western media. And they had this construed story about a Greater Serbia. But on page 228, paragraph 1, in your book, you say that from that time on, that is to say from the 25th of April - and you mean 1993 - onwards, "Milosevic in formal terms gave up the idea of a Greater Serbia and strove for an agreement under the conditions that the majority would be able to accept in the UN. And in the next two years, he never wavered from seeking a solution of that kind. Unfortunately, the demonisation of Milosevic in the USA reached such levels that the administration Congress and the media, without any difference between them, were incapable of adapting themselves to this new reality and continued to say that Milosevic was attached to the idea of a Greater Serbia." So on the basis of the fact that I advocated the Vance-Owen Plan and later on peace plans and took an active part in seeking a peaceful solution, your conclusion is that from the 25th of April, I did not advocate a Greater Serbia after that time. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the relationship to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Some people have a different interpretation about Kosovo, but I believe Kosovo was part of Serbia and still is part of Serbia unless and until the UN Security Council makes a different delineation of Kosovo. But I believe you had given up the idea that the only way to get a settlement was for that part of Republika Srpska in Bosnia-Herzegovina had to be geographically linked to Serbia and Montenegro. You still wanted very close linkage, but you didn't, in my view, and all the plans that you supported thereafter always had the Bosnia-Herzegovina's boundary maintained, the same boundary that had been accepted by the Security Council in May 1992 as the definition of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you are saying that I was not advocating a Greater Serbia from the time and point at which you became included and involved. And you have no knowledge or awareness whether I had ever strove -- striven for that idea before. Do you have any knowledge of that or was it just propaganda? Do you actually know that I was or not?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Knowledge is a difficult thing to point a specific time, but the impression I had up until January of 1993 was that, all things being equal, you would have preferred a division of parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that you would have preferred a portion of Bosnia-Herzegovina to be in part of Serbia and Montenegro and a portion of Bosnia-Herzegovina to be in part of Croatia. If you ask can I prove it, have I got factual evidence of that, I have to say no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The passage is at 153 in the paperback.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe, Mr. Milosevic, that you are a pragmatist and that in our discussions in Geneva in the start and development of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, and I think even earlier than that in your discussions with Mr. Vance, I think you had come to recognise that though it would have to take place over a long period of time, the Croatian Serbs would probably eventually have to live within Croatia. I think you had not come to that view of Bosnia-Herzegovina until some way into the discussions. And I think that when you met with President Mitterrand in Paris, I think that was a very important meeting in that I think you realised that if you could get a settlement in Bosnia-Herzegovina, President Mitterrand would put the weight of France behind lifting of sanctions, and indeed he gave you a specific promise that that's what he would do. And from that moment on, I think you began to see a way through which would satisfy your beliefs of what the Serbs needed but would not mean breaking up Bosnia-Herzegovina. But these are my interpretations of your views, and they may well be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you're not quite right in so much as you have any idea of my pushing the idea of a Greater Serbia, and this general term Greater Serbia is a creation of the Austro-Hungarian Empire after the annexation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because everything that was Serbian was called Greater Serbian, whereas nobody ever of the politicians, Serb politicians and those who were within the power structure ever came out with any ideas or programmes for a Greater Serbia. And anyway, in that same passage and paragraph in your book, you say: "As far as Milosevic is concerned, the Bosnian Serbs have protected their interests, and in that sense, they have become victorious, but it wasn't a Greater Serbia in the sense of a unified country from Belgrade to Banja Luka and Knin, and from our January meetings in Geneva, this wasn't important." So you mention that in January that it wasn't a question of Greater Serbia, that it was not Greater Serbia in terms of one country reaching from Belgrade to Banja Luka. So you -- and Knin. So you base them on propaganda waged at that time, I assume, and on the stories told and bandied about by Milan Panic and not on any objective argumentation that you could have had. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are pretty sweeping allegations, but the difference between you and President Tudjman is President Tudjman never made any secret at all that he disliked the existing map, that he did not consider that the map of Bosnia-Herzegovina was correct, that it had never been an independent country, shouldn't be an independent country, and he wanted to go back to the old Badovan [phoen] map. Now, that was his view. You did not express that view in any way in those terms, but that didn't mean necessarily that you hadn't got a similar view. I can only hear what you say is your view, and I've heard it more concisely than I'd heard it before in the negotiations. I just -- I take note of your view.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but Lord Owen, let's take a look just to remind you. This is Cutileiro's map for the division of Bosnia according to the cantonal division on the basis of the 1971, 1981 and 1991 population censuses. And here we see white for the Serb territories, Croatian for the striated ones, and the Muslims are the black areas. I'd like to draw your attention to that. So this then is Cutileiro's plan, signed by all three national or ethnic communities, and we supported it ourselves, and from this it is evident that at the time of Cutileiro's plan, when that took centre stage we were talking about territory, the kind of territory that could not be referred to as being Greater Serbia in any way. That then is Cutileiro's plan, and the map accepted by the Serbs and signed by Izetbegovic and Karadzic and Boban, and all that took place Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. before the conflicts broke out. And there wouldn't have been a war anyway had we stuck by Cutileiro's plan. And we can see from this and from those times that there can be no mention at all of Greater Serbia. It is a map within Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state, and the Serbs accepted it too. Radovan Karadzic signed it. And Izetbegovic, once he had signed it, withdrew his signature at the proposal of Warren Zimmermann, and Zimmerman, in his book, says he prevailed upon him to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must have a question. Is the point you're trying to make that this plan is illustrative of the fact that you were not a supporter of Greater Serbia? Is that the point that you're making?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This demonstrates that the leadership of Republika Srpska, led by Radovan Karadzic, by its support and signing of this plan had no idea of any kind of Greater Serbia. But the Cutileiro plan related to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. Let the -- no. I'm going to stop you going on. It's time that the witness had an opportunity to answer the point that you're trying to make. Lord Owen, if you want to comment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think that this is a perfectly reasonable view for Mr. Milosevic to put forward. This demonstrates that my timing of his conversion against Greater Serbia, or maybe he never had the Greater Serbia, it's evidence that it's reasonable for him to put it through, because it is true, of course, that they did accept the Cutileiro plan. The Cutileiro plan, when you look at it again, you can see has the problems of whether it could have provided a cohesive government for Bosnia-Herzegovina. But I'm not against what Ambassador Cutileiro tried to do, and much of that is reflected in the provincial map of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was the ten provinces that was the basis of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. So this may be and you're certainly open to convince people that you were never in favour of Greater Serbia and this would be part of that evidence. I understand that. That doesn't mean that I am personally accepting your interpretation of that history. I think there was an aspiration held not just by you but by many Serb nationalists that there could be a different map, and of course theoretically there could have been. And at various stages in the negotiations, President Izetbegovic himself became quite interested in a Muslim state within the confines of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The exact shape of it was never discussed if for no other reason than it was beyond the terms of reference the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia. Our terms of reference given to us in August 1992 were to find a peace settlement within the internationally accepted boundaries of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I have already indicated that I think that was a remit which was unnecessarily rigid and they ought to have been prepared to look at boundary changes much earlier. But this is all the history. It's obviously important, but it also is a history when I was not in office and I therefore can't add more to what lay behind the Cutileiro map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Lord Owen, certainly it was possible to draw many other kinds of maps. This was drawn by the three parties with the assistance of Ambassador Cutileiro. But the very fact that Radovan Karadzic and the leadership of Republika Srpska signed up to it, and this meant an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina and division into cantons which under no circumstances has anything to do with an idea of a Greater Serbia is surely sufficient proof that that idea was not at the basis of the policies pursued even by Republika Srpska and even in those days of the Cutileiro plan. Before the war, before the outbreak of any conflict, before anyone was killed. Isn't that certain? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're a great one for asking leading questions, Mr. Milosevic, but I do not deny that if you were making your case which you have never believed in Greater Serbia, if that is the case, this is a concrete evidence that certainly my statement that you only really accepted that it had gone in April 1993 might be wrong and that you had accepted it was a lost cause earlier than that. I can't be more helpful than that to you, and you are perfectly entitled -- this is the whole issue of this court, is that you must be given and are being given a fair trail and you must be able to make your case. And you may be able, when you come to give your own evidence, to develop this. I'm not standing in your way on this issue. I put my view in April 1993. Perhaps that was too narrow a view of somebody who had only come into the detailed negotiation since September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I am emphasising here that as you see, even Radovan Karadzic did not advocate a Greater Serbia because he is the one who signed it. The leadership of Republika Srpska signed the Cutileiro plan.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But, Mr. Milosevic, you and I know that Mr. Radovan Karadzic signed many things, and if we took on the basis that everything he signed was his intention and what he wanted, then of course we wouldn't be in this mess. The fact of the matter is that he consistently took positions in one forum which were different from positions he took in other forums. It is perfectly possible to have signed this map as part of a view and later wanted to bring together all those areas in the Cutileiro map that are white, which represent Serb majority areas, and to bring them into one republic. I also think it's perfectly possible that Mr. Radovan Karadzic at one time had seen Republika Srpska linked to Serbia and then, as he grew more and more confident of his position, wanted to keep Republika Srpska outside Serbia because he didn't share much of your own ideology. It's not for me to go into the mind of Mr. Radovan Karadzic, but I think I am entitled to say that I am allowed to have the utmost skepticism of documents that are signed by Mr. -- Dr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Your skepticism is something you're entitled to, but you remember that when the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was formed in April 1992, a declaration was adopted in which the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia declared urbi et orbi that it had no territorial claims towards any one of the former Yugoslav republics. When it adopted its own constitution, the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is, when Serbia and Montenegro formed the FRY. I am sure you know that.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you would not then follow the logic of that declaration and recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you know we spent many hours discussing why you would not recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina. And had you done so, I think if Serbia and Montenegro had recognised the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it would have made life much easier in the negotiations, even though you would have qualified it that the government should be formed on a different basis. But I don't want to go through your time on this issue, but you made that declaration, but you didn't follow its logic, which was the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina under international law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Surely first the political settlement needed to be found in Bosnia-Herzegovina first. You yourself say that the government had control over only 10 per cent of the territory. Who could treat as a partner a government that has control over only 10 per cent of its territory? We insisted on a political settlement which would equally protect the interests of all three peoples and their agreement. And later on, when peace was achieved, do you remember that Izetbegovic and myself, benefiting from hospitality of President Chirac in Paris we normalised relations, he recognised the continuity of Yugoslavia as Tudjman did before him at our meeting in Athens. Unfortunately, the new authorities threw that all overboard and requested that Yugoslavia be readmitted to the UN, but that's another matter. So when things were settled, when the parties had agreed, when the interests of all three nations were recognised, there was no dispute. Up until then, things were at issue. Wasn't that logical, Lord Owen?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was how you saw it, but as you know, the Contact Group attempted for many months to get you to recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you used all those arguments that you've used now to refuse to do so and said that you would not do it until there had been a final settlement. So you have stayed consistent to your arguments, but there were many of us who thought that a recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina with the qualification about the government would have been a way of putting to rest, if you like, the propaganda which, as you see it, of Greater Serbia. Certainly I believed it was in your interest to make that qualified recognition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But that government that you are speaking of committed the greatest crimes against the Serbs in those days, that very government. It wasn't a Serbian, Croatian and Muslim government, it was a government that had committed the greatest crimes against the Serbs in those days, even though you say that Serbs crimes were greater. But anyway, that will be established. That was the government responsible for the greatest crimes against the Serbs and against the Croats, for that matter, in the period that you just mentioned in 1993 and 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I wonder if we're going any further forward by going over this topic in that way. Have you got something else you want to ask the witness? Because time is running out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I quite agree with your quotation that I was eager for Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia and anywhere else to protect their vital interests and nothing beyond that, and those interests are protected if they are treated on an equal footing. But I hope you will agree that the notion of equality implies that if Serbs are equal, then the others have to be equal too, and vice versa. So please tell me, did I ever ask for the Serbs living anywhere more than that they should be equal with all the other peoples throughout all the conversations we had over a period of three years?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This word "equal" is a tricky word. I'm not trying to be too pedantic, but it is my belief that if we had had more goodwill, we could have arrived at a solution in which the Croats in Croatia would have been able to continue to live there. And although this -- we are focusing here on Bosnia-Herzegovina, it does need to be remembered that one of the biggest ethnic cleansings in the whole of the Balkans during this period was that involving Serbs who had to flee Krajina in the early summer of 1995 and that, when we talk about this whole complex of problems, we have to recognise that one of the biggest failures was the failure to ensure that the ordinary citizens in Croatia who were Serbs were entitled -- were able to continue to live there. Now, we did devote quite a lot of time to that issue, and we were never able to make the Croatian Serbian leaders show the degree of realism which was necessary to protect their own people. And there were occasional leaders who were ready to do that, but -- so you -- I don't think I can help you any further than that. I think you were trying to protect and ensure equal citizenship for Serbs in Croatia through the UNPAs and the initial Vance Plan, but they themselves didn't help themselves. I mean, the months that we spent in 1974 -- 1994, 1995, trying to get an economic agreement was one in which was extremely frustrating in which it was very difficult to get an understanding in Zagreb of the necessary concessions that were necessary, and also in the Knin. And in many ways, the Knin leadership showed less understanding of the rights and of the -- their obligations to their own citizens, and they got -- the consequence was this mass ethnic cleansing of Croat Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now that you yourself have touched upon that topic again, I shall just read to you a quotation from Thorvald Stoltenberg in September this year when he was there on a visit, and who refers to those events that you mentioned just now. He says: "In the negotiations between Knin and Zagreb prior to the Operation Storm, in which Franjo Tudjman took part too, I suggested that SAO Krajina remain within Croatia but with the right to self-determination. Both sides accepted the proposal, but the reply was valid for only a couple of hours, because Tudjman was already preparing orders for an offensive with the acquiescence of the Americans. I note that the UN did not know of the preparations of the Croats nor of the approval of the White House for the Storm. When the offensive started, I felt cheated, and what I said is the only truth." This is what Mr. Thorvald Stoltenberg said. Is that true, Lord Owen?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but it wouldn't surprise me if that was said by Thorvald Stoltenberg. Thorvald was my partner in the negotiations as the UN representative once Cyrus Vance stepped down, and he was a remarkably honest, straightforward political leader, and he was at great pains to make clear, particularly when he was the UN representative responsible for UNPROFOR and was in Zagreb, as well as being co-chairman of the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia, great pains to make clear the obligations of the world and the UN to the Croatian Serbs and that they should be treated fairly. And I'm afraid by then it was very clear that President Tudjman had won the heart, if you like, or the intellect or whatever it was, he had won the -- around the Americans to his point of view and that was a reality. But again, it was in desperation that they didn't find it possible to get a dialogue and a settlement in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that they came round to accepting that the Croatian armed forces would tilt the balance of power inside Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is what they did in the fighting that took place in the summer of 1995. And if you're looking for the realism that came out, that eventually in the Bosnian Serbs led to Dayton and your own participation in Dayton, one has to admit that part of that came from the defeat of the Serbs by the Croatian army in Western Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Surely it resulted from our peace efforts, Lord Owen.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think the reality was that even General Mladic had to face up to the fact that the Serbs were by then beginning to lose the war, that the fact that the West tolerated the Croatian army fighting overtly inside Bosnia-Herzegovina meant that the balance of force had tilted against the Bosnian Serbs and the Croatian army was helping not just the Croatian Serbs but also the Bosnia-Herzegovina government forces. So that the -- when you came to the NATO bombing in August, end of August and September, early September, there had been a very different balance of forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I think that meant more realism from General Mladic. It nevertheless took him two weeks of bombing before he came right round to it. But you know these areas better than me. I was no longer a participant, I was just a very interested observer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That was the choice between war and peace. What would have happened if Yugoslavia had got involved like Croatia had? Then the whole of the Balkans would have gone up in flames, and that precisely was the greatest contribution made to achieve peace, and that is how the Dayton Accords were reached. And after all, to be quite honest, Serbia made the greatest contribution to those accords, because without Serbia there wouldn't have been any Dayton Accords. Isn't that correct, at least?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that is undoubtedly true. I also think you are correct in saying that if the Serbia and Montenegro, the FRY, if their armed forces had crossed into Bosnia-Herzegovina, then we would have had a very bloody war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So we made the option of peace.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe you wanted peace. Yes, I've said already from April 1993 onwards you supported all the different propositions. What I wished you'd done is made it, your verbal support for peace, you had made that into a -- the military pressures and economic pressures that we talked about yesterday which could have brought a peace very much earlier. I believe you put up with the Bosnian Serbs' obstruction of peace for two years -- two and a half years too long. Now, some --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Lord Owen, let us be correct in dealing with the facts. I do believe that you are a person who is correct with facts. Now, look at those peace plans. The Cutileiro plan was dated March 1992. The Serbs adopted it. Then for a long time there was nothing. But there's an entire correspondence that I don't have time to go into where Serbs insist in communication with Carrington and Cutileiro that the negotiations continue even though Izetbegovic withdrew his signature. So the plan was March 1992, then the Vance-Owen Plan in May 1993, and surely it follows from this -- or it appears that you are reproaching me for not having resorted to some more drastic measures in favour of the Vance-Owen Plan as if I had abandoned it but in fact you abandoned it. And I don't mean you personally but I mean the international community. The Vance-Owen Plan was abandoned in the first place by the Americans, or rather they didn't even support it. They didn't want to support it. Isn't that true? And they made it known to the Serbs that they didn't consider the plan to be a good one. And then we from Belgrade acted as Don Quixote who advocated the plan which was being undermined by the international community and among that community the largest world power. Isn't that true or not?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a great deal of truth in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, Lord Owen, when was the plan that you named "Invincible," after the carrier, that we referred to as the Owen-Stoltenberg plan? Anyway, it doesn't matter what its name was. When was it, though, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In September 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In September 1993. In May there was the Vance-Owen Plan. All our efforts and pressures. It is immediately abandoned and already in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. September the Invincible Plan is put on the table and again the Serbs accept it. There was the red zone, during which we are bringing pressure to bear from May until September, but then the international community abandoned the plan, appears with the Invincible Plan which again the Serbs adopt and the Muslims reject. Wasn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think the international community abandoned the plan. The European Union took over the plan of three republics and called it the European Action Plan and increased the percentage of territory for the Bosnian government from 33 -- 30 per cent to 33.3 per cent, and that plan was on the table in December 1993, and we've earlier referred yesterday to the fact that that was probably one of the best opportunities for a peace settlement, which might have been much easier to bring reconciliation than even the Dayton plan. I think the boundaries have been established between the Muslim -- predominantly Muslim republic and predominantly Croatian republic would have given a great deal more stability to Bosnia-Herzegovina. But that was not agreed, and the agreement there was a difference of about 0.5 per cent of territory between Mr. -- Dr. Karadzic and President Izetbegovic, in Brussels. Then came the Contact Group plan in September -- sorry, in July of 1994, and then Dayton in 1995, all of which you can say that you agreed with, but in order to get agreement, we had to have agreement on the map, and there the Bosnian Serbs were at times difficult to the point of blocking, and a settlement which would normally have been accepted by reasonable rational people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Lord Owen, I agree with you. It was crazy even to imagine for a plan to fall through for -- because of 0.5 per cent of territory. It is absolutely beyond common sense. But something must have been behind it. But this is why I'm referring to this chronology. There's the Cutileiro Plan in 1992, then the Vance-Owen Plan in 1993, then the Invincible Plan in September 1993, then the Action Plan Kinkel-Juppe, or rather of the European Union, then the contact group, then Dayton. The Serbs accepted the Cutileiro, Invincible, they accepted the Action Plan of the European Union, and they accepted Dayton. Therefore, to be quite fair towards the leadership in Pale, they accepted four peace -- [French on English channel] -- isn't that correct, Lord Owen?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [French on English channel]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're getting French on the English channel. Can we try again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall I answer, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are making -- you're aligning your own support for all those plans with the position of the Bosnian Serbs. The Bosnian Serbs rejected the Vance-Owen Peace Plan in Pale. The Bosnian Serbs did accept the Cutileiro Plan, the Bosnian Serbs did accept the plan on HMCS Invincible and many of us believe that President Izetbegovic, when he was returning to Sarajevo, was going to argue for its acceptance as well, but the EU Action Plan never reached final agreement. There -- we could not impose a settlement, and we were trying to get the two sides to agree. The Croats were agreed to it. Indeed they had agreed to all these plans, but the area of difference, as you say, was not 0.5 per cent, and it was within the power of Karadzic and Krajisnik to have made that adjustment. And as you say, it was crazy that they didn't. And then in Dayton, as I understand it, you were given the casting vote in the delegation of the Serbs, and you did reach agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Will you let me just make a correction. I didn't prevent the voting of the Serbs from Bosnia, but having learnt from some very bitter experiences that both you and I are aware of, before we went after Dayton, I drew up an agreement. And this is the agreement which was final and which you are probably familiar with. It was signed by Karadzic and Koljevic and Plavsic and Krajisnik and Kosic - I don't know what he was - Prime Minister Buha, and Mladic. And on the Yugoslav side, Lilic, Milosevic, Bulatovic, Kontic, the Federal Prime Minister, a second Bulatovic, the Defence Minister, and the Chief of Staff. And also by the Serbian Patriarch Paul. Why? Because I didn't wish a repetition of Athens and the Vance-Owen Plan rejection, and because I wanted to have a document in my hands which would provide for the possibility of a final adoption of what is adopted in Dayton, that there can be no review of it. And should the votes be divided, because it was 3-3, three from Republika Srpska and three from Yugoslavia, then I would have the casting vote. Because in the three, of which I was one, my vote would be decisive. And this was precisely to avoid the dangers that we have referred to. You are surely aware of that. I didn't prevent them from voting, but in Dayton, an agreement was reached which was feasible and which in relative terms protected the interests of all three nations. Isn't that so, Lord Owen?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is. It's not entirely a joke when I say that I wish that you'd had a casting vote in Athens and that we had had the patriarch of the Serbian church there to witness that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to adjourn now. Mr. Milosevic, we've considered your time, which is now up, but as an act of grace, you can have another quarter of an hour when we come back. We will adjourn. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood it correctly, Mr. May, you've given me an additional 15 minutes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Lord Owen, with respect to these plans, and I seem to feel that we need to clarify this question of an Action Plan that you referred to a moment ago. I should like to remind you of one of your quotations from the book. 407 is the page of the English version which I have on the compact disk, where you say the following: "There had now been four lost peace initiatives [In English] the Carrington Cutileiro plan before the war -- before the war started, the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, the Invincible package, and now the EU Action Plan. Most Europeans I judged felt any further effort while the US remained on the sidelines was doomed for it allows the Muslims to escape the necessity of compromise inherent in any negotiation." [Interpretation] Do you therefore consider that for the lack of success of the Action Plan of the European Union it was predominantly the Muslim side that was to blame, including the United States?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe that. I think that President Izetbegovic faced an extremely difficult issue on agreeing on a map which was effectively defining a Muslim republic, predominantly Muslim republic, which was part of the essence of the new structure that we were on. We'd abandoned the provincial structure which you could argue was based on the cantonal Cutileiro, the provincial Vance-Owen Peace Plan, we were now going for a recognition that there would be three autonomous areas within Bosnia-Herzegovina. And on that map, we were accepting that these three enclaves in Eastern Bosnia were very tightly drawn. We'd expanded the areas a bit. We'd got a link, a road link, through to Gorazde, and we got Zepa and Srebrenica together, but they were very tight. So in Eastern Bosnia, there was a real serious problem for President Izetbegovic in convincing his own people. And secondly, there was a real problem -- sorry. That was in Eastern Bosnia. And there was, secondly, a real problem in Western Bosnia where he did need, I think, more territory. And as I say, the person who had the territory was Dr. Karadzic and the republican Serbian leaders. The person who had the least territory, given that they were the majority population -- not the least territory but the lesser territory than the Serbs was the Bosnian Muslims, and I think it was not unreasonable to get that 0.5 per cent out of the Bosnian Serbs. And you stayed late that night, and I think you left Brussels thinking that Karadzic and Krajisnik would come up with this extra 0.5 per cent the next day, and they didn't. And I think that was -- that was their call, really. They had to move a bit on both those two rounds of territory to get the EU Action Plan agreed in Brussels.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, without doubt. And I think that you and I and everybody else couldn't have even supposed that something could have been started on the basis of 0.5 per cent of the territory. That was quite clear. But I reminded you of this quotation of yours precisely because it speaks about this position taken by the US allowed the Muslims to avoid, to sidestep the need for a compromise, which was necessary in the negotiations. So that was the point of the quotation I selected from your book.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on that I agree, and I had been advocating privately for quite awhile that the format of these negotiations, European Union and United Nations, was insufficient and that we had to involve the United States. And I had been -- I advocated in the subsequent months that we should do more through NATO, and I was a strong proponent of the Contact Group Plan which would allow the EU representation to be subsumed in the membership of Britain, France, and Germany, the Contact Group. But the crucial extra element in addition to the Russian Federation of the Contact Group, to make it five, was the United States. And from that moment on, the United States became a partner on the negotiations. The Contact Group Plan was actually very little different from the EU Action Plan, and indeed not much different from Dayton, to be honest. The 51 per cent for the Republika Srpska was there in all of these plans, the EU Action Plan and before HMCS Invincible. Now, the 51 per cent began to be something which the Americans accepted and then they had the Croat-Muslim federation. So I do believe it was crucial to involve President Clinton's administration, and from that moment of the formation of the Contact Group Plan we began to be more coherent in our own Western position. And in order to do that, as I say, we had to make the EU representation come through its three largest countries, and I think that was realism.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was realism and that isn't at issue. But what I would like to do now is go over certain questions having to do with the fact that you speak about certain errors, mistakes that led to the civil war and the premature recognition of Croatia and Slovenia, among other things. Is it without doubt, Lord Owen, that it was only in Yugoslavia that all the nations, all the ethnic groups, realised their right not to be broken up into different states and that they could live in one state, all the Serbs, the Croats, the Muslims, and that life in that one area of Yugoslavia, one country Yugoslavia, had a series of advantages for the citizens living in it on different levels, and why did states form a European Union anyway? So I don't suppose you're challenging that.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think it would have been easier if the former Yugoslavia had not dissolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely what I'm talking about too. The former Yugoslavia was an advantage and advantageous to all its nations or ethnic groups, and I assume you are aware of the fact that a series of states, international organisations, personages supported Yugoslavia's integrity and strove at the beginning of the Yugoslav crisis to safeguard its unity, to preserve it.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the position of the United States, and President Bush Senior and also under Secretary of State James Baker, and that was also the position of the European Community.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure you also know that the European parliament on the 9th of June, 1991 adopted a resolution on Yugoslavia which did not support the unilateral acts of secession on the part of Slovenia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not actually aware of it, but if you tell me so, I have no reason to disbelieve it, and it would be consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the Council of Ministers of the European Community and the European Council, also organs of the European Community supported the territorial integrity of the SFRY, and on the 26th of March, 1991, the European Community proclaimed a declaration on Yugoslavia in which it stressed that, "A united and democratic Yugoslavia had the best chances of becoming integrated harmoniously into the new Europe," and I'm quoting that from that particular declaration.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you also know that the Council of Ministers of the OSCE meeting in Berlin on the 19th of June, 1991 adopted a declaration too? Amongst other things, it expressed support to the territorial integrity and unity of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And now as we're talking about this about-turn, let me remind you of what you say in your book, in actual fact the English version on my compact disk on page 46, paragraph 1, right after your appointment, and you write about that, you say: "On Sunday we went off to London by car and stopped on the way to have tea with Peter Carrington at his farm in Buckinghamshire. As always, Peter was relaxed, but in his voice while he was talking and saying how the European foreign ministers behaved towards him, there was a certain sharp note. There was no doubt that the decision made by the EC on recognition of December 1991 he considered that to be treachery, betrayal. And while he presented the chronicle of events, I asked myself out loud --" this is what you say -- "What could they do to me? And he laughed." And you go on to quote him: "Don't worry. Nothing much remains that they could do." So Carrington considered that this recognition put paid to the peace efforts; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He wrote to that effect in a letter putting his views on record more formally, and so did Cyrus Vance and so did the then-Secretary-General of the United Nations, Perez de Cuellar. So the three people most involved in the peace process at that time all opposed the European Union -- European Community's decision to recognise, believing apart from the merits of the Slovenia and the Croatian question is that it would be inevitable that they would move on quickly to what they considered to be a premature recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina; and that is exactly what happened, and I believe it was a very serious mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I would even go as far as to say tragic, Lord Owen, and I'm sure you'd agree with that. Now, do you remember a statement made by James Baker on the 13th of January, 1991 before the American Congress when he said that, "The fact was that Slovenia and Croatia unilaterally proclaimed their independence. Despite our warnings they resorted to force in order to take over the border crossings, and this gave rise to a civil war." That is what James Baker said at a hearing before the US Congress on the 13th of January, 1991.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it but I have no reason to doubt that that's what he did say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And I'm sure you'll remember Cyrus Vance's statement on the 9th of February, 1995, when he said the premature recognition of the former Yugoslav republics was a terrible mistake.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was his view, and he held it right until he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "What should have been done was to keep to The Hague agreement, which did not allow for recognition of the former Yugoslav republics while an all-embracing solution was found. This was not respected, and I think it was a terrible mistake," and that is a quotation of him. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of it, and I agree with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Lord Carrington, in the Vienna weekly Profile says the following, speaking about attempts to reach peace. He said, "In that business I helped Cyrus Vance who was the main negotiator. The negotiations developed well and we were almost -- we had almost reached a solution to Krajina and Slavonia. However, at that point the European Community at the end of 1991 decided to recognise Slovenia and Croatia." And he goes on to say that, "The behaviour and conduct of the European Community toppled the peace conference," and I'm quoting him there. And I go on to quote, "Croatia, by being recognised, got what it wanted. So did Slovenia and they no longer had the desire for continuing the peace conference. And what is more important, this same thing should have been enabled for others, Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the first place. But Alija Izetbegovic did not opt for anything other than independence, although it was clear to him too that this kind of option would mean war. Hans Dietrich Genscher wanted to have international recognition of Slovenia and Croatia. Practically all the rest were opposed to that." Then he goes on to criticise the journalists, Lord Carrington does, and says he was being blamed for being pro-Serb. And his answer to that was, "That's senseless, that's nonsense. It wasn't easy to say who was good and who was bad. When the Croats proclaimed their independence, they did not allow the Serbs in their own country, and there are 600.000 of them, to have any guarantees whatsoever. It was understandable, therefore, that the Serbs were concerned over this if we bear in mind the Croatian and Muslim Ustasha conduct during World War II." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. You must be responsible for that quote, and Lord Carrington's perfectly capable of being responsible for his own quotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember something that the Diplomatico published about, that Chancellor Kohl, at a summit meeting in Brussels on the 29th and 30th of June, 1991, in fact, that is to say four days after Slovenia and Croatia had declared their secession, although it wasn't a topic on the agenda, called for the instantaneous recognition of those republics.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certainly aware that that was his view, but exact words I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know what was going on on the 16th of December, 1991, at the EU summit where Genscher stated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. There's no point, really, asking the witness about matters that he can't deal with. Now, you've had your quarter of an hour. You can ask a few more questions providing they're relevant and they're matters which Lord Owen can answer. Mere propaganda on your side isn't going to help us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not engaged in any kind of propaganda. What I'm trying to do is to speak about the facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And you will have the chance to do that when you give evidence, of course, but the only point is to ask a witness questions which he can actually deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]
