utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, on page 556 and 557 of your book, you say that, "Lord Carrington and Perez de Cuellar, in letters, drew attention to the fact that premature recognition of Croatia could fan the flames of the crisis to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and a step -- they went a step further." And you say the following in paragraph 1 on that page, 556, 557: "The mistake that the European Community made to recognise Croatia could have been Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. overcome had the situation not been complicated by the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina regardless of the consequences. The USA at the end of the December 1991 were opposed to the recognition of Croatia and became a very active advocate of recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992, the spring of that year. However, we need not have considered this to be unavoidable nor was it logical to carry on and recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina. Internal Yugoslav republic composed of three large constituent nations with very different attitudes and positions with respect to independence. Therefore, they went from one mistake to the next." But the price that was paid was human lives, Lord Owen. So therefore, as you yourself linked up the wars that you describe and call it one war, a war against Yugoslavia, a war in which Yugoslavia was dissolved, would that be right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was a profound error to go ahead with the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina just because you'd recognised Croatia and Slovenia. And certainly to do so in the absence of a substantial UN peacekeeping force in the country prior to recognition. So you could have at least reduced the dangers of war breaking out. One of the problems was that the United Nations at that stage were having difficulty in getting sufficient number of troops from contributing countries to uphold the United Nations Protected Areas, four of them, in Croatia. So in a way, our problem was, which was there throughout the whole of this crisis, this marvelous habit of politicians making rhetorical commitments in the Security Council not backed up by the forces and the resources on the ground. And that, unfortunately, has been the story of the former Yugoslavia and no more so than over Srebrenica where we gave the impression of being able to protect people without having the qualities. There is not the fault of the United Nations. The United Nations is frequently used as being the overall umbrella to blame. The blame has to be on the Security Council at the time, and in particular its permanent members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Lord Owen, you mentioned General Morillon, and from what you write about him, I have gained the impression that you have a good opinion of him. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure you know that he testified in the French parliament, and I have here the authentic text, L'audition de Generale Philipe Morillon October 1992, 1993, et cetera, et cetera, in the French parliament, and as Mr. Nice asked you some questions about Srebrenica, although you said you weren't there at the time and you didn't want to go into it but he insisted upon it, in this document he says: "I did not waiver in stating and writing that Mladic had fallen into a trap in Srebrenica. He expect resistance which he didn't encounter. So I don't think he expected the massacre to take place, but in that regard he underestimated the amassed hatred. I do not believe that he ordered the massacres. However, I don't know. That is my personal opinion." And it is also my personal opinion and I can't believe it. You too have met General Mladic, so I assume that you can't believe that he could have ordered a dishonourable thing of that kind.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid here we come to a very serious disagreement. It's not job to claim or make a speculation as to what happened in Srebrenica in 1995, but it is certainly my job to tell you, Mr. Milosevic, and the Court that I don't share that view of General Mladic. I think there was many different elements in the character of General Mladic which made him a very ambivalent personality to determine, but I do not consider that it was beyond General Mladic's record of behaviour to have been complicit in massacres of Muslims. I believe he was a racist, I believe that he had many quite irrational attitudes to the Muslim population, and I believe that his record as a general demonstrated that there was a callousness and a brutality about the man that would have allowed him to make decisions. Whether he did or not I do not know, and I'm not prepared to speculate. But as to his character, I would not be a character witness for General Mladic's inability to conduct or to -- to -- I'm searching for a word which is not necessarily conduct but to acquiesce in a massacre of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Lord Owen, I quoted Morillon and said that I too don't believe that he ordered the massacre, and that is what Morillon says, that he doesn't believe it either. But let's move on. Speaking about what you knew from 1993 or, rather, what he knew on the basis of 1993 and Morillon's testimony in parliament and the amassed hatred, Morillon adds: "I informed Belgrade too. I went to see Milosevic and told him this is what is going to happen. He helped me. What I -- that I had won that battle then that was thanks to the position taken by Milosevic, but New York was also kept au courant." So I assume you know about that as relating to 1993.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I made it quite clear, and many people don't like me saying it, but I do believe that you were very helpful in 1993 in stopping General Mladic going in and taking Srebrenica. And I rang you up personally. You were also under many representations of other people, and I believe the record is quite clear that you did intervene and you were of considerable help in that situation. I think you were well aware of the great danger for the reputation of the Serbs. If they had gone into Srebrenica, there would have been very bitter street fighting. The grudge match that existed around Srebrenica between -- over Bratunac and others would have spilled over into a very, very nasty scene. And I do not know what representations if any were made to you in 1995 or what were the circumstances. As I say, I was no longer a negotiator. But I think it is the most shameful single episode to have occurred in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the massacre around Srebrenica in 1995, and inasmuch as I must have in some ways contributed to that by not alerting enough people, by not being -- making it more and more apparent how dangerous the situation was, I deeply regret it. But I can only tell you I opposed the safe area policy from beginning to end. I considered it was a fraud. I said so. I made it clear to ministers. I opposed the joint action plan in 1993. I earned the very considerable animosity of the United States in doing so. I think it was a disgraceful decision. Every single member of that Security Council, when they passed the resolutions on safe areas, knew that they were not going to provide sufficient troops. They knew that the UN generals had said that there should be a minimum of 35.000 new troops in order to conduct that policy. We did not provide those troops, and we are in part responsible for that appalling massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I completely share your opinion about that. And there was nothing more shameful that could have happened or anything that was so detrimental to the people who were the victims but also to the detriment of the Serbs. And that is why I am interested in seeing that what happened in 1995 is dealt with and light thrown on it as clearly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, you have five minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. Yes, I am bearing that in mind, that you very generously gave me some more time today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, as to this testimony before the National Assembly of France, Philippe Morillon presents his views about another issue that you touch upon in your book and your statement. And Marileno Daubaire [phoen], a deputy, asked him, "Do you consider - yes or no - that there existed the aggressor and the victim of the aggression and that the victims were to be protected?" And General Morillon said, "No. I was present and I experienced and lived through that crisis from its very start in April 192 and I always refuse to believe that there was the aggressor and the victim of the aggression. And because of that, the Bosniaks criticised me for a long time." As opposed to Philippe Morillon, you yourself were not in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the beginning of the war but you came some six months later, but nevertheless on the basis of your own experience and knowledge, can you say that you agree with General Morillon with respect to that assertion of his?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is two simplistic to see the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina as being one of aggressors and victims. I've made it quite clear that I think there was evil done on all sides by all parties. The political leaders demonstrated a lack of compassion, of consideration, and readiness to compromise on all sides. But nevertheless, there is a danger in trying to be fair in apportioning an equality of guilt, in trying to determine that all were equally at fault. That, in my judgement, was not the case. I said it yesterday and I say it again. In trying to make that very difficult judgement as to how many -- you know, what was the balance of fault, what was the balance of horror, what was the balance of inconsiderate behaviour, I think the Bosnian Serbs come out the worst. I they are followed by the Croatian Serbs, and then by the Muslim leaders and troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean the Bosnian Croats.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Bosnian Croats. Yes, sorry. The Bosnian Serbs were the first, in my view, in the scale of bad behaviour. Secondly were the Croatian Serbs -- the Bosnian Croats, sorry, and the second were the Bosnian Muslims. But -- you know, I'm not God. I'm not here to apportion these things, I'm just giving my overall estimate because of this tendency for a propaganda war with each side claiming that only they were the ones who were fair-minded, only they were the good people, only they were the reasonable ones. Unfortunately, it's necessary, it seems, to form some judgement on this whole affair, but we are better looking at individual episodes, but it was one of the problems that things were never quite what they seemed. On the face of it, crimes looked as if they could be associated with one element, but there was a good deal of agent provocateuring, so you had to have a skeptical view as to who was responsible for any particular thing. But I think your fellow Serbs did not do the reputation of the Serbs worldwide any good by their conduct in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you're mentioning those incidents and the erroneous image, let us take the explosion at the Sarajevo Markale marketplace on -- in 1994, on a Saturday. That was one of the turning points in that particular war, and the Serbs were blamed for it. Isn't that right? Whereas you, on page 419, speak about the fact that a delegation of the Bosnian government which was to have negotiated - and this took place afterwards - did not appear at the Sarajevo airport. "Rose was angry, furious. He went to the Bosnian Presidency to try and persuade President Izetbegovic and his military commander General Delic to come and attend the meeting. And those around General Rose never hid the fact that at the meeting he said to the leaders of the Bosnian Muslims that he had just received technical information indicating that a mortar shell did not come from the area under Serb control but from the Muslim part of town. "If this information were to be circulated by the media, the outcome would be completely different, and if the -- Izetbegovic tries to withdraw from the negotiations, he, Rose, would feel duty-bound to conduct the preliminary evidence of the investigation conducted by the UN." That is something you write about on page 419 of your book. "If the government negotiating team does not attend the meeting on the 17th of February at the airport, he would convene a press conference." And that is the end of your quotation. So the knowledge that the Muslims shelled their own people was something that was not brought to light but used as a method of coercion despite of the fact that public opinion was engulfed by an anti-Serb hysteria. Isn't that right, Lord Owen?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you are partially correct, but unfortunately, you have not completed the story. At the request of Dr. Karadzic, and indeed it was inevitable anyhow, there was a full-scale independent inquiry of that particular mortar incident, and the UN inquiry that was established by Boutros Boutros-Ghali came to the conclusion that they could not pinpoint who was responsible, whether the shell had been -- mortar had been fired from a Muslim army controlled area or whether the Bosnian government forces or whether from a Serb forces. But where you are correct in saying is that in the early stages, the preliminary evidence did point to it coming from an area of Sarajevo controlled by the Bosnian government Muslim forces, and it was in a most extraordinary situation to live with watching NATO and the European Union all ready to make decisions on the automatic assumption that this had been fired by the Bosnian Serbs. And that was, as I say, never proven, nor, however, was the converse proven, that the original impression that it had come from the Bosnian government Muslim forces. So it's left as an unsatisfactory episode, but in the diplomacy of that period it was extraordinarily important that the United Nations retain their integrity and their impartiality and it is to the great credit of General Rose that, despite endless public criticism, he refused to do so. And I think it needs to be said in this court that many UN personnel lost their lives in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in fighting for impartiality and in fighting against very powerful forces. At that time there was a readiness amongst the European Union, which I must say I was not proud of, and of NATO, to come to one conclusion and that was that this was totally the fault of the Bosnian Serbs. But nevertheless, again the background which NATO had to face and the European Union had to face is that day after day, there were shells landing in Sarajevo from Bosnian Serb mortar sites, and guns firing into it. I myself stayed with General Morillon and were woken in the middle of the night by artillery fire directly on the UN headquarters in Sarajevo. So there was a background history. And though that particular episode there was a danger of the impartiality and integrity of the international community being damaged, fortunately it was not, and the establishment of the fact was they couldn't conclude who had fired it, but they knew that there were too many heavy weapons in placements around Sarajevo which had been endlessly firing into Sarajevo, and they had to go. And so an ultimatum was put on General Mladic that those forces had to be withdrawn, quite correctly. And General Mladic refused to withdraw them. That was the reality. He rotated them round out of Sarajevo and then back in through other roads. And it was only when the Russians at initially our instigation but then very quickly and quietly moved their forces, UN forces committed in Croatia, around through into Sarajevo and reinforced that part of the area of Sarajevo to give reassurance to the Serbs, and then your own generals forced General Mladic to start to withdraw his troops -- to withdraw his heavy weapons. And we managed to establish an exclusion area in Sarajevo and eventually to have, for quite a number of months, peace in Sarajevo with very few scattered incidents. But it soon broke down. I only go into that in some detail. They things -- the facts are very difficult to establish, but what I've said I believe to be an accurate interpretation of a very difficult ten-day, 14-day period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you have had past your time, but you can ask one last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If it's just one more question, and as you are talking about my political positions, Lord Owen, I noted down that you said yesterday with precision what I was expressing was the majority Serb opinion. What else should I have represented except the majority opinion of the people who had elected me?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic, whether or not you were elected in the Western democratic sense is open to some argument, but nevertheless, at times there has never been any doubt in my mind that you were the chosen leader of the Serbian people. You represented majority opinion. So I'm not going into the electoral process, but I do believe you did represent for a substantial period of time the views of the Serbs. That puts a very special responsibility on a political leader to sometimes be prepared to lead his public opinion against their views, to tell them the truth, to lead -- to take a minority position. And I think that my great regret is that you did not take on that view, that Serbian nationalist view, particularly over Kosovo but on some other aspects of this dispute, and I don't think it is sufficient as a justification to say I was acting always on behalf of majority opinion. Democracy is not purely and simply a continuous referendum in which leaders are meant to represent the opinion of the majority. It is extremely important that they are prepared to stand, at times, for views and opinions that represent minority. And what is right internationally and what is right in international law should be upheld, and I think that you had a responsibility to uphold those international laws even if that was not what was accepted by majority Serb opinion. I'm sorry if I end on a sort of lecture note, but the reality of political leadership through history is that some of the greatest acts have been when leaders have been prepared to run against their own public opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's Mr. Kay's turn. We'll deal with any exhibits you have at the end. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Lord Owen, I'm going to ask you some questions now based on our Court Exhibit C18, which is your book Balkan Odyssey, so I'll be taking Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. pages from that. And if we could turn to chapter 3 at page 94, which is the section dealing with the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. And this is in January of 1993, you having entered the peace process in September of 1992. And in that period from the September to January, obviously you researched the background, information, had meetings to decide a course of action that you were going to put to the principal parties involved. That would be a correct summary, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Looking at the plan at page 94, we see there what were the constitutional principles, defining Bosnia-Herzegovina as a decentralised state and then giving substantial autonomy to provinces but denying an international legal character to those provinces. So the point was on your peace plan at that moment was the recognition that the international community had already given that Bosnia-Herzegovina was going to remain a recognised state. There was no backtracking on that issue, and it certainly wasn't possible to backtrack on it by then.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's correct. That was the terms under which we were set up from the London conference. And anyhow, that was international law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Within that decentralised state, you weren't going to identify the particular ethnic groupings of the provinces that were going to be contained within.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't -- we didn't ascribe an ethnic basis in the names or in our own description, but nevertheless it was always obvious, given the situation in the former Yugoslavia, that people would claim that certain provinces were or were not likely to have majorities within it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In January of 1993, at that stage the Bosnian Serbs were in the most powerful position.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They occupied about 70 per cent of the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The recognition of the peace plan at that stage would have made them give up substantial gains that they had made of a military nature over the previous year.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were being asked to withdraw from something like 23 per cent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So it was a very substantial reversal of the product of war, if you like, or of ethnic cleansing, and it was to be done by negotiation without being forced. So it was -- it was ambitious, there's no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At page 97 of the book, you make it clear that you were asking a victor to give up a larger proportion of land, which is something very unusual in a historical context.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They would have to retreat from about 38.6 per cent of the territory which they occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you challenged any critics of that peace plan to recall in history any episode similar where a controlling force could have been so generous.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, that's true. I can't think of any case where they had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Putting this into context in relation to Mr. Milosevic in Belgrade, for him to adopt the support of that plan, you would probably recognise would have represented a considerable political challenge for him in dealing with the Bosnian Serb leadership.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I did, but we were asking not just him. At that particular time President Milosevic was president of Serbia and we were also involving the authority of the president of the FRY, President Cosic, who was a well-known nationalist, and also President Bulatovic from Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At this stage when the peace plan was unveiled, if we look at page 99, you mention there that there was great criticism by Izetbegovic, President Izetbegovic, as to the plan itself, and there was the use of a propaganda machine on his part to reflect that he was almost being bullied within this process to accept less than he was entitled to.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, actually, we had heard that the Bosnian Muslims had accepted the plan. In fact, I think it was former Ambassador Zimmerman who had been told that. And we also got that impression. But it's true, of course, that they then did, sensing the new incoming American administration, thought for some strange reason that this plan was soft on the Serbs, they were naturally enough wanting to try and get more territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You've come to the point that I was going to deal with next, that in fact your view was, if we look at page 100 of the book, that there was a certain degree of misrepresentation by the US State Department encouraging Izetbegovic to ask for non-negotiable territory against the Bosnian Serbs almost as a means of causing a failure of the peace plan.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was really deliberate. I think it was they didn't understand the plan. They didn't understand the history at that time. They were a new administration taking office, but there were people, of course, who did understand it, but there was a very strong feeling amongst some people in New York and elsewhere, and Washington, that we had been too generous to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You write at page 100 that Vance and Okun had been complaining of US misrepresentation of your intentions and the details of the plan.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And some of the feelings behind this were believed to be because the Russians supported the plan and the US was wary of a Russian-backed initiative.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may have been a factor. That may have been a factor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And again when we consider Mr. Milosevic's political history, he of course was a communist, he was from a socialist party, and his government had good relations with Russia.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were beginning to be a bit strained, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. But that was a future within it.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a -- I don't think the Russian Federation at that time were as supportive as the Serbs, as sometimes the Serbs thought they should be as fellow Slavs, but nevertheless, I think it was a tribute to the then Russian Federation foreign secretary Mr. Kozyrev that he did try to be fair-minded throughout this whole period, and I think the Russian Federation played an extremely helpful path right up to the Dayton peace conference and beyond in working with NATO in implementing the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: To be bold about this, there is a lot of tub thumping that's been going on, but political interests were also being served by the states who were looking at these affairs externally.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't live in a perfect world.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we turn to page 102, given the difficulty of this plan as it was to be received by the Bosnian Serbs, Mr. Milosevic's backing to that plan was an important key on your behalf.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time in January, we didn't have his total support, but he was acting helpfully in trying to -- he saw what we were trying to do, establish the principles of the cooperation, and I think somewhere in the book I mention that he came up with the idea of merging two principles and presenting nine principles instead of ten or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's the middle of page --

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He provided the basis for a compromise which Karadzic could say that he proposed eight principles, the co-chairman proposed ten principles, and we had now settled for nine principles, and it was a rather ingenious suggestion, which we were grateful to accept from President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's the middle of page 102. "Milosevic suggested over lunch the face-saving formula."

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And again, you were obviously able to recognise that there were important political consequences for him as well in helping put forward a plan that was contrary to the aspirations of the Bosnian Serb leadership at that time.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You have to remember that most of the opposition parties supported Dr. Karadzic, including some of those who later went on to be leaders of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia after President Milosevic lost the election.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And to balance this, back in Belgrade you were aware again of his need to carry this through the politicians in Belgrade in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to a point. This was not a working democracy as we know it in the West, but he had to take account of the criticism of his plan that was coming whether it was coming from Draskovic or Seselj or any of the other leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: One of your ways of assessing his commitment to this plan was the understanding from the evidence that Karadzic then began to try and sell the plan to his constituency.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would certainly have helped if he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He was trying to represent it as being a victory on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. His acceptance of it.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It was quite the reverse. Karadzic was hedging his bets on the plan throughout and saying this would be a great defeat for the Serbs, that they would have to give up all this territory and that they were giving up territory which had industrial locations on it, that they were giving up precious territory. Karadzic reversed it, Karadzic never accepted the plan and he didn't want it. And you know, the reality of life is that Dayton gave the Serbs six per cent more territory than the Vance-Owen Peace Plan gave them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In your book at page 103, you make it clear that it was the pressure by Mr. Milosevic, then-President Milosevic, on Mladic and Karadzic and the other leaders that this plan had to be adopted.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he pressurised, and he got them to sign up for it in Athens, but they then denounced, went back on the signature, including, really, Dr. Karadzic in Pale. Dr. Karadzic went nominally in support of the plan in Pale, but I think what reports I've heard of his speech, it was done in such a low key way that he was already effectively helping those who were going to vote against it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You described Karadzic breaking down and caving in at the eleventh hour in relation to the Vance-Owen Peace Plan.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Athens, yes. He -- they negotiated through most of the night with him, and that was not just President Milosevic but it was President Cosic and Bulatovic and also Prime Minister Mitsotakis, the Greek Prime Minister. He played a very helpful role.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again, these were key steps taken by Mr. Milosevic in support of the peace plan to attempt on his side, on the Bosnian Serb side, to get them to that commitment.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No doubt he was -- he -- well, I have no doubt that he was totally committed to it and that he didn't go to Pale and go through a subterfuge of trying to pretend that he was selling them a plan and letting them vote it down. He suffered quite a humiliation in Belgrade of not being able to get his will through in Pale. That's my reading of it. There are others who, as I say, have a conspiracy theory about this but I don't think that's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You describe him at Pale as having been defeated, only collecting only two votes and the other party collecting, I think 51 votes or something like that, and him leaving by a side door.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wasn't there, but yes that's the description in the papers and that fulfilled -- I think that was the case, and the crucial intervention came from General Mladic and also Mrs. Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just to balance this now, in that January when this peace plan is being pushed forward - just looking at page 105 of the book now - the last thing you needed to keep the Serbs on side was President Tudjman unleashing a military attack on the Croatian Serbs to try and take land.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was extremely unhelpful and no doubt designed for it. I think he felt that the world was focused on Bosnia-Herzegovina and the peace plan, and it was a good opportunity to get his military action in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And also at this time again, the Clinton administration were being -- or taking steps that you believe actively were trying to kill off the Vance-Owen Peace Plan.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were focused on Croatia. I don't think they were -- you know, this is a new administration coming in. I think President Clinton came into office on the 20th of January. The 23rd of January or around there the attack on Maslenica bridge was launched, so I don't think that the Clinton administration could have been expected to have a view on that very much, that Croatian aspect, but they were -- they'd already indicated pretty clearly that they were unhappy with the Vance-Owen Peace Plan in the weeks up to the inauguration. And as you know, under the American system, the election having been held in November, the two-month period that goes from November until the inauguration in January is usually made with a bipartisan policy in the State Department. The State Department accommodates to the incoming presidency's views on foreign policy, which is perfectly reasonable and understandable system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You described at page 114 that the new administration had already made up their minds and were intent on killing off the VOPP.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no doubt that was what they were doing, and the issue for me and for Cyrus Vance was whether or not we acquiesced in this. It was particularly acute one for Cyrus Vance because, A, he was American, and B, he had been former Secretary of State, and his previous deputy, Mr. Warren Christopher, was now the Secretary of State. So for Cyrus Vance to go into open opposition to a new incoming democratic administration which he obviously had some sympathy with was very difficult indeed, and so we discussed it and it was agreed between us that I would take the full frontal attack on the American administration and he would support me, which he did absolutely solidly. They tried to make -- this was an example of a very difficult question. We could have acquiesced in this and let this issue ride, or we would challenge them. It seemed to me my responsibility for the European Union, which was united on this, that we were not saying to the Americans take it or leave it to this plan, what we were saying is give it serious consideration, don't reject it outright. These are your allies, your friends who have come to this proposition in the framework of a conference in which America was represented and which the Russian Federation and other non-EU countries were represented, and we were not prepared to see the plan sidelined without a fight, so we fought it. And we did manage to get them to nominally support the plan a fortnight later or perhaps three weeks later. But it was never full-hearted support.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Taking it briefly then from that January until May when there was the Pale meeting, you were aware of the fact that Mr. Milosevic kept up his pressure on Radovan Karadzic, you describe as bullying Radovan Karadzic to accept the plan and to accept the reality of political life.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, bullying which I totally supported on that particular occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Page 158, 159.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You were of the view that Karadzic here was giving no leadership. He was unprepared to see through his constituency within the Bosnian Serb political grouping and challenge them to come on board.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You had, and you describe them at page 163 at the Serb Assembly, Biljana Plavsic, who was a hard-liner, opposing signatory to the plan; Krajisnik, and Karadzic was more concerned with his own leadership of the Bosnian Serbs than trying to get through the peace plan.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think we began to see Krajisnik emerging as a powerful influence. He was at Athens, but he was basically sidelined and didn't play a major role, but post Pale, I think Krajisnik became a more influential person, and thereafter I think one had to consider Karadzic and Krajisnik basically as one. It seemed to me that Karadzic had decided that he would -- he wouldn't move far without Krajisnik on board.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just looking at page 165. This isn't concerned solely with the political dimension but also the military dimension of the political situation. You had General Mladic, who was a powerful figure at this stage, almost running his own political agenda, not controlled in every sense by the Bosnian Serb parliament but able to exert his own influences and have his own alliance within the political groupings of that parliament.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think Mladic became very powerful from then on. And that's not to say he was powerful as a military leader, but I think he began to have a political constituency from the Pale Assembly onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The position that you were left with then in the May was that Pale could reject Belgrade and get away with it.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And buck the rest of the world, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Because they -- they were able to present a substantial force within the area, and they had a cohesive political agenda on their own terms.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As the vote at the Pale Assembly showed.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You have to remember these people were not of the same political party as then-President Milosevic, and they had a different view of Serbian history. I think it's true to say that Karadzic began to see himself as a sort of Mihajlovic Serb, a different tradition from Tito and from the Partisans.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Quite capable of having his own thoughts of his own kingdom, if you like, divorced from Serbia. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He may have believed he could from time to time, but then I think one of the things that happened from Belgrade is they reminded them every now and then of how vulnerable they were if they didn't have the support of Belgrade. And you come to this whole question of the supply line through from Serbia Montenegro to the Bosnian Serbs, that when they did get above themselves I think they were pulled back to the realities that they were dependent on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But there was the problematic issue, though, back in Belgrade in how you control the Serbs who were there in Bosnia. You can't attack your own people. The political agenda would not have permitted that.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we discussed this yesterday, and I was quite open about my view, that it would have been unrealistic to ask President Milosevic at any time to put the forces of the JNA onto the Bosnian Serb military. Now that was not the realm of practical politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You've got to recognise here the ethnic connections between the various peoples and --

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And they were also, all of them, both Belgrade and the Bosnian Serbs, were appealing. The Bosnian Serbs because they were ideologically rather proud of the fact that they were not communists, although quite a number of them had been. Their relationships were a bit more ambivalent with Russia but there were opposition forces to President Yeltsin in Russia that were going and siding with the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You had recognised by this stage, in May of 1993, that President Milosevic was not a magic bullet that you could just fire and get what you wanted.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could fire certainly not, no. And nor could many other people. No. He -- he had his limitations on him, and that would be absurd to not recognise, but I've already made it clear I think he exaggerated those limitations on his power. Whether deliberately or not, I don't know. He won't be the first politician to be extremely cautious about exercising power when it means damaging your base. Politicians tend to look after their political base.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. This stage thereafter from the May saw a great degree of political uncertainty. There was the savage phase of the Muslim-Croat war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You refer to that at page 171.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And shifts in policy from the US, page 180. Originally seeking more land for the Muslims and then wanting more land for the Serbs, a complete contradiction in points of view.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was extraordinary. By May we had the US administration that had condemned the Vance-Owen Peace Plan as being too generous to the Serbs arguing that there should be more land made available to the Serbs, that the plan was unrealistic, it was too harsh on them. It was amazing circumstances. However --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the Russians who were originally content then wanted to back more land for the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's hard for the Russian foreign minister, when confronted by an American Secretary of State who wanted to make more concessions to the Serbs, saying to them, "No, thank you, I think we should be tougher on the Serbs." That was not a realistic position for Kozyrev to adopt at all. So I have no criticism of Kozyrev when offered this joint action plan even though I think he saw some of the problems with it. It was perfectly understandable he should have gone along with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And this was encouraging the respective parties to seek to try and fulfil their own interests?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Even if it was at the expense of a cease-fire or peace. They realised that the land was up for grabs. A land grab started.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think if you -- that type of people, rather bullies and fairly immature in political view, if they get concessions, they see that as a licence to demand more concessions. And the West's attitude to these different plans -- and I want to stress that the Vance-Owen Peace Plan is only one plan, and in many ways an ambitious one. What was the most important plan of all was the Contact Group Plan. This was put together by five of the major governments of the world. The fact that they walked away from their map and didn't impose it gave tremendous surge to Karadzic and Krajisnik and Mladic to think that they could defy Belgrade, defy everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again, at the time of that Contact Group being put together and their plan being -- emerged from the political quagmire, President Milosevic wanted to see that the Contact Group was in fact serious, because there had been so much vacillation and change it was difficult for anyone to really follow who was being serious and who was not.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I don't know quite what you're referring to, but if he did think that, which is a perfectly reasonable thought -- I certainly thought that myself. I didn't know whether they were serious or not. I don't think they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 309 of your book is where that conclusion can be drawn.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've read the book better than I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Meanwhile, because President Milosevic had backed the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, his authority had been undermined with the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's -- that was true. I think were some very interesting phases in President Milosevic's power over the Bosnian Serbs. I think he was initially pretty powerful and you got the feeling that they were taking it, so when I first met him he was a powerful influence. I think there was a period after Pale where to some extent he had been weakened by asking for support and then it disappearing. And you know, the plan disappearing, so to speak. So I think he has a grievance that we were not supporting our own plan at one stage. Then I think in September 1974 [sic] the decision to start to restrict supplies across to the Bosnian Serbs was an attempt to recover lost influence, and my own estimation -- I said 1974; 1994. I think that probably by 1995, and certainly by the summer of 1995, he had recovered a good deal of his influence which he wielded, as we heard today, of getting himself into a position where he held the casting vote in the negotiations prior to Dayton. And I think by then they had lost the Krajina and the Bosnian Serbs had seen reality. The Serbs had been ejected from the Krajina. The Croatian government was in a -- overtly operating in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that was tilting the balance. The Bosnian Serb armed forces numbers were being reduced. They were having some restrictions. We can argue about how much, how effective those restrictions were, and I think then-President Milosevic's powers were probably greater, and he exercised them, and he exercised them as anybody who has read Richard Holbrooke's book on Dayton, right at the very last moment over Brcko, and that was an issue he and I had discussed in greatest detail months -- over many months. The position he took over Brcko was predictable. That was the position he had basically taken in the negotiations over Brcko up in the north where the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So there is a continuity to all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He, for that period, from May 1993 until the summer of 1995, had seen --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to avoid any confusion because of dates, this meeting at which the leadership of Yugoslavia, upon my initiative, reached agreement with the leadership of Republika Srpska regarding a unified delegation in Dayton was held on the 29th of August, 1995. It was the 29th of August, which means long after the events in Bosnia and Croatia, at least several weeks later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, until that period of May 1993 until August 1995, he had gone through a period where his power had waned and Karadzic was very much in political control of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And/or Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's difficult --

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That position was upheld by a large number of people. This is not just my own view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those people who were closest to the negotiations, whether it was General Wahlgren, whether it was the Russians, some of the Russian experts, a large number of people who were involved in that did believe that there had been a waning and a waxing in President Milosevic's influence, and I agree with your analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Indeed, the Russians were giving direct support to President Milosevic to try and influence Karadzic and exert pressure upon him.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, the Russians had appointed -- the Americans had appointed as part of the sort of new American initiative when they came to grips with the Vance-Owen Peace Plan right back in February 1993, they appointed Ambassador Bartholomew, a very able diplomat, and tough, as their representative. And the Russians had responded by appointing Ambassador Churkin. And Ambassador Churkin was tireless in his efforts and visiting on the ground, trying to influence all the different Serb factions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Page 307 of the book. Also in this period, you of course have the NATO airstrikes in, I think it was May of 1995. Notwithstanding that, after the NATO airstrikes, President Milosevic still supported the Contact Group plan.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 330. Karadzic still being very much in control, President Milosevic politically making what you would have considered to be a bold position, no doubt, despite the NATO airstrikes, to still be backing the Contact Group peace plan.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He certainly continued to back it, and I think he had doubts as to how much they were ready to certainly bring pressure to implement it. And of course at this time he believed that the sanctions should be lifted from him, from his country. And this was a very, very difficult question, and there were divided views even in the European Union on it. Broadly speaking, the European Union felt that we ought to have sticks and carrots and that easing of sanctions on Serbia and Montenegro was a reasonable thing to do to reward the cooperation that we were getting from Belgrade. The Americans broadly took the view that if you ease sanctions you'd never get them back, and therefore sanctions had to be held firmly over the FRY. There was a legitimate argument, therefore, in terms of international diplomacy as to how to handle that, and there are arguments on all sides. But it still made it difficult for President Milosevic at times that the West seemed to not be prepared to give a reward for them in that sanctions were affecting the standard of living and employment prospects in Serbia, Montenegro, and no doubt made difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And just considering that, you have the attack on the Serbian Krajina by Croatia, page 343 of the book, after Martic had closed the highway, and President Milosevic was very frustrated, as it seemed, that that could be the cause of losing a chance for peace and the Contact Group plan.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, President Tudjman by then had shown that he had judged the political situation rather well from his point of view. He came -- he provided the Americans with an alternative route, and he knew he could get away with attacking there. He was not helped by the fact that this so-called leader of the Krajina Serbs, Martic, was a fool. And unfortunately, there was another person called Mikelic who was much more reasonable and serious, and if his voice had been dominant in Knin, it would have been possible to conduct these negotiations. But the Croatian Serbs were absurdly provocative in closing the highway, and they gave an excuse for Tudjman to launch an attack which was of course out with international law and a breach of agreement over the UNPAs. But he got away with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And as part of the complexity of the situation, you were very skeptical of the dog that didn't bark, being the forces of the Bosnian Serbs, and Karadzic had been able to come to an arrangement with Tudjman who supplied him with oil.

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'm sorry just to laugh, but it is -- it was almost a farcical situation. I think I wrote to Douglas Hurd - I think it's in my submission - that if it's possible to conduct a strategy in a cesspit, a delicate strategy in a cesspit, this is what we were doing. It was an unbelievable situation. So here was the FRY, President Milosevic, applying sanctions on to the Bosnian Serbs, putting his oil tankers through to the Croatian Serbs, may or may not be off-loading some oil en route, who knows, perhaps not, and then encounters President Tudjman authorising supplies to Karadzic and the Bosnian Serbs, at which stage what does he do? In order to recover some influence, he probably supplies a bit more oil to the Bosnian Serbs. You know, when I sometimes read about and hear the comments of people about this, they have no idea of the extraordinary circumstances in which we were operating, all this time with UN Resolutions and Security Council things which were mutually contradictory, frankly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And Tudjman had expressed to you that that accommodated his interests and he was quite prepared to do it against an old enemy?

utterances.speaker: DAVID OWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He had the great advantage that he was absolutely clear what he wanted. He wanted total control over Croatian territory, and he didn't mind how he got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Lord Owen, that brings your evidence to an end. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I -- I'm not sure I'm allowed to make a comment, but I think the last period of questioning vindicates your decision, presumably, to allow a friend of the Court to take place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Pack, there's a housekeeping matter we've got to sort out before we begin the evidence. Mr. Milosevic, you've got various documents which you handed in. You want us to exhibit them, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I handed them over to the registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll just have a look at them one by one. The first one we have is a copy of the Cutileiro plan. If that hasn't been exhibited before - there certainly have been a lot of references to it but I don't remember an exhibit - we'll give that the next D number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D209, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The next document is the letter of the 27th of November, 1991 from the accused to Mr. Cyrus Vance. Give that the next number. Next D number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 210, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is then the interview with General Morillon, which is in French. We'll just consult on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will admit that, giving it the next D number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 211, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there some other document that you were going to put to the witness but didn't have time? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there were some other ones, but I think that I will be able to use them with some other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Yes, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is B-1531.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I address you very briefly on one administrative matter, which is that B-1524 now will be the witness coming after Harland. He was scheduled originally for last Thursday, but that is the order in which the witnesses will run tomorrow and next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It may be that we won't get much beyond Mr. Harland tomorrow, but we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the witness would stand, please, to take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: May the witness be shown, please, the front page of tab 1. May be witness be shown the B/C/S version of the statement, front page at tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, looking at the front page there, are your details, name and details as set out on that page, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: I can't hear anything. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I will repeat the question if necessary. Witness, are your personal details, your name and personal details as set out on that front page, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, have you given two statements to the Prosecution, dated the 25th of June, 1996, and the 28th of June, 1997?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown, please, tab 2, and the front page of the English version statement at tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, can you confirm that that's your signature there at the bottom of the first page of the English version of your statement dated on the 28th of June, 1997.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Turn to the fifth page, please, of that statement and confirm if that is your signature on the fifth page, the last page of that statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: May the witness please be shown tab 3, the front page of the English version statement at tab 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That is your statement appearing on that page; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Please look at -- please look at page 9 of that statement and confirm that that is your -- again your signature on page 9, the last page of that statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, have you had an opportunity to read both statements whilst in The Hague and prepared an addendum statement yesterday, 3rd November, which sets out the changes that you wished to make to the first of those statements and some additions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown tab 1 again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: The B/C/S statement at tab 1. If you just look at the last page of that statement page. Is that your signature again appearing at the last page of that B/C/S statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, do the --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: -- contents -- Witness, are the contents of the first two statements, with the changes and additions that were made and set out in the addendum, taken together, are those statements true and correct to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask for those three statements to be admitted in evidence and assigned an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 581, Your Honour, under seal, confidential.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no questions. I'll just read a summary of the evidence. The witness was a senior figure in public life in Foca at the time the conflict broke out there. He describes the build-up of ethnic tensions in Foca. He says that Velibor Ostojic, Petko Cancar, and Vojislav Maksimovic were in Foca quite a lot in the year before the war. During the first half of 1992, they were in Foca all the time. They were giving orders for the paramilitary and volunteer forces from Montenegro and Serbia as well as certain formations of the JNA. The witness describes meetings attended by Ostojic, Maksimovic, Cancar and Stanic, president of the SDS in Foca, at the church in Cerazuluk in Foca. The Serbs had their Crisis Staff there. In 1990, the foundational meeting of the SDS in Foca was held. Petko Cancar was one of the persons in charge of the organisation of this meeting. The Focatrans affair was going on at this time. Serb workers had left the Focatrans company and had been striking for several months. They blocked streets inside the town and stopped normal relations between citizens in Foca. The workers were directed by Miro Stanic at the local level and by Ostojic Maksimovic and Cancar at the republic level. They met regularly with the strike committee. The SDS leaders encouraged the Serb workers to create their own company and also created such feelings in the Serb populated villages. The witness describes the distribution of arms to Serb civilians in Foca. He recalls one occasion about six months before the war when a Muslim policeman stopped two long vehicles containing military, infantry, and heavy artillery. On the 6th or 7th of April, all the Serb policemen in Foca were called to a meeting with Ostojic, Cancar and Maksimovic chaired by Miro Stanisic at the hall where the SDS had their offices. The Serb police were given ultimatum at this meeting to separate from the Muslim police. Thereafter, all the Serb police left the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Serb and Muslim police were divided albeit sharing the same building. The witness describes negotiations between members of the SDS and the SDA which started around this time. In the witness's view, the negotiations were just a way for the SDS to gain time. The armed attack on Foca began on the 8th of April, 1992. The witness describes the barricades which had been erected by Serbs on all the approaches to the city. There was one Muslim barricade in Donje Polje set up as a response to the Serb ones. On the first night of the attack the witness heard a lot of shooting and firing. Serb paramilitaries had artillery and machine-gun fire directed against Muslim parts of Foca. The witness could tell that Donje Polje and Sukovac were targeted by artillery fire. There was some resistance but it was sporadic and limited. From the 13th of April Serb paramilitaries occupied almost all the town except Donje Polje. The witness was later told that directives for anything happening around Foca were coming directly from Radovan Karadzic and that Cancar, Maksimovic and Ostojic were acting on his behalf, passing on orders to local leaders like Stanic. After the first day of the attack, the witness left Foca town and went to Ustikolina From there, sometime after 19th of April 1992, he went to Gorazde. Your Honour, I have no questions to ask of this witness. Might I alert Your Honours to the matters which I set out on the first page of the proofing summary. This witness has security concerns, and I invite the Chamber to hear evidence in private session which he fears will tend to lead to his identity being revealed to the public, and I've identified the sort of issues which may lead to his identity being revealed to the public at the front of the proofing summary and then throughout the proofing summary in the highlighted portions of that typed text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And one thing, Ms. Pack, although we admitted the -- all the statements including the addendum, I note the addendum was produced only yesterday, and it contains substantial changes and addition. Given that the accused received it only today and he had no time to prepare for it, so I think some changes, additions, important part of it should be dealt with live or at least you give some explanation to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. The position was that this witness was, by an order of the 10thth of October of this year, granted -- his evidence was to be admitted under the Rule 92 bis procedure and the Prosecution didn't then take a declaration in view of the Chamber's earlier indications to that effect a couple of weeks ago, that that wasn't necessary. The addendum statement is similar in scope in fact to the addendum statement that is ordinarily obtained when the 92 bis procedure is followed, albeit that there is that substantive matter in paragraph 8 that is slightly lengthier in scope than would ordinarily be contained in an addendum statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness should deal with that orally, if necessary in private session, paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour. If we can go into private session then just to deal with that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. 1531, in the introductory summary, Ms. Pack at the very outset said that you were a well-respected person in the political life of Foca. So I assume that you have a good knowledge of all the events dating back to those times. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: I think that the lady in question said in public life, in the public life of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. I noted down in the political life of Foca, but public life if you like. At any rate, you were respected, a respected man in Foca. So we're not disputing that, are we?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: No, we're not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Fine. Now, you talk about the situation in Foca prior to the outbreak of the war in 1992 and immediately after it broke out, and from what you say, it would emerge that the Serbs were preparing for war while the Muslims were not. Now, do you claim that that's how it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: I wasn't involved, nor do I have any information as to the Muslims' preparation for war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You weren't involved in that you say. All right. Now, were the Muslims arming themselves before the war broke out, and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: I can't either say yes or no to your question because I don't have the necessary information on that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, is it true that on the 25th of August, 1990, a large SDA rally was held to promote the party in Foca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date, but yes, a rally to promote the party, the SDA party, was held in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was that meeting attended by 150.000 people, roughly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: I think the figure was a little lower, but yes, a large number of citizens did attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say somewhat less, how much less? If not 150.000, how many would you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: Well, there were over 100.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And is it true that amongst them there were about 20.000 people from Serbia, Muslims from Serbia, in fact, and from Sandzak led by Sulejman Ugljanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: There were a number of people from that area, but you're quoting a large figure and I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What would be your rough estimate then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: Well, I can say what I'm sure about, and one of the people who were there was the man you mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me then, how many inhabitants did Foca have before the war? What was the population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: About 42.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in that town of approximately 42.000 inhabitants, as you say, the presence of -- if we take this lower figure, this conservative estimate that you say is over 100.000 people, in such a small town at a rally, would you say that that represents a tectonic upset?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: Well, a large number of people came from the interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Transport was organised by buses and coaches, and they were put up in different areas for them to be able to attend the rally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And can we observe that on the political plane, the Party of Democratic Action in Foca started in full force, very intensively? Could we put it that way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: I don't share your opinion on that score.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in a town of 40.000 inhabitants, you have over 100.000 to attend a rally to promote a party, and as you say, came from all parts, from Serbia, from Sandzak led by Ugljanin. So is it possible to conceive of any more than that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: When we're talking about the situation in Foca itself, it all began earlier, in the first half of the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you now about this particular rally, and we noted, you and I, although we don't agree on the figures, but the general figures are not contested, so I'm asking you whether activities of a party of this kind in one place implies the fact that the party had a very great stronghold in that particular locality, or foothold? Just say yes or no to save time, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: At that promotional rally, as far as I can remember, it was stated, among others things, that it was being organised to commemorate the victims from World War II so that history should not repeat itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 1531, I'm not asking you what was stated. What I'm saying is that a large -- an enormous rally of that kind, and you yourself admit to there being over 100.000 people attending from various parts of the country including Serbia, the SDA party there, that Foca was a great stronghold of the party in that place, in that town; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: Well, I can say that there were individuals from Foca who were activists of that particular party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well, Mr. 1531. And there were also individuals who were party activists among those 100.000. I think that sounds highly convincing. But never mind, let's move on. Is it true that the Cengic family was the number one and highly respected family in town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: I could say that the Cengic family was highly influential when it came to the political life of the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the head of the household was Halid Cengic, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Halid's son Hasan Cengic was arrested in 1983 and convicted together with Alija Izetbegovic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you happen to know that the two of them were tried for extremist Islamic political views; where Izetbegovic was concerned, this was expressed in his Islamic declaration of the 1970s.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: I haven't had an opportunity of becoming better acquainted with the document, but from the media, I read that they were convicted for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what they were convicted of and for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: Well, what was publicised in the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was the Islamic declaration where Izetbegovic says there can be no peace and co-existence between the Islamic faith and the non-Islamic faith and its institutions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that. I haven't read the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. 1531, if you say that you are an influential and respected individual in political life, was it possible that as a prominent member of the SDA party you had no knowledge of the contents of a document of that kind written by your president?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: I wasn't a member of the SDA myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, do you know the fact that the declaration was published again in 1990 in Bosnia-Herzegovina, second publication, and that it played a significant role in Izetbegovic's pre-election campaign, in fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The motivation for condemning Hasan Cengic was the same as Izetbegovic's conviction, because of extremist positions. And they were convicted together with some like-minded individuals.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: Yes, I know that they were convicted in the same legal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the course of the 1990s Hasan Cengic, for example, became a high-ranking functionary, official?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: I know as much as was written about the topic in the media, that he was among the leadership of the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he was vice-premier of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: No, Hasan Cengic was not. That man was Muhamed Cengic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, did Hasan Cengic have a title of any kind and position in the Islamic religious hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know about that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the time before the arrest and conviction of Cengic in Foca, was that a point of support for Alija Izetbegovic's illegal activities before he was arrested? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In your second statement you speak of a strike and protest of workers in the Focatrans company in 1990. The strike and protest officially were socially motivated, but you attribute political motives to them, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: Everything that was happening at the time and after that points to such a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Workers usually go on strike for social reasons. Now, tell me, what would be the alleged political motivation for that strike?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531
utterances.text: Workers of Serb ethnicity in Focatrans in the first half of 1990 left the enterprise compound, and I think they took some of the means with them, and they presented their demands, and I remember that one of them was an ultimatum to have the general manager replaced. I know that this went on for months and that as early as then there were preparations for the formation of nationalist parties so that some people who were frequently in touch with the strikers and the strikers' committee later, after the elections, I saw that they had emerged into the top leadership of the SDS and had important positions in the executive powers of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So I know that during that period of the strike, inter-ethnic relations were seriously upset, that support was given to those people, and every effort was made to prove that joint life was impossible, though I do remember that they were called on repeatedly to go back to work.
